overview: Mapuche histories encompass autonomous communities, exchange and creative work across southern South America. Relations with neighbours changed over centuries. Colonial resistance and later dispossession belong to this history alongside farming, family knowledge and living artistic traditions.

periods.title: Reasserting autonomy
periods.summary: A major uprising expelled Spanish settlers from much of Mapuche territory. Local communities continued to organise their own affairs, rather than forming one permanent monarchy.

periods.title: Frontier exchange expands
periods.summary: After the mid-seventeenth century, commerce across the frontier and movement toward the Pampas reshaped economic and family relations. Exchange accompanied, rather than simply replaced, conflict.

periods.title: Occupation west of the Andes
periods.summary: Chilean military campaigns advanced through Mapuche territory with forts and new settlements. The conquest of land changed livelihoods and political authority; it did not end Mapuche identity.

periods.title: Makers reinterpret museum collections
periods.summary: A museum project brought Mapuche specialists into the study of objects in its care. Their accounts added language, practical knowledge and cultural meaning to collection records.

items.text: The lof organised related families. In the historical model described by the National Library, a longko led a local group with limited authority. Wider alliances could form during war without creating a ruler with permanent jurisdiction over every community.

The same account describes local leaders allocating fields to families and reassigning plots while depleted ground recovered. Reserve land provided another resource. Access depended on social relationships as well as cultivation, and arrangements changed under later restrictions.

Textile specialists Matilde Painemil and Cristina Manquepi contributed family histories and practical knowledge to the museum’s collection study. Their expertise connected the handling of old cloth with forms and meanings still understood by makers.

The textiles discussed include makuñ mantles, headbands and chañuntuku, thick woven saddle coverings. These are distinct objects for dress and other uses, rather than interchangeable examples of a single decorative pattern.

Painemil describes design as mental and creative work, sometimes connected with dreams. She also teaches classes and makes commissioned textiles. Her account presents weaving as a skilled livelihood and an ongoing artistic practice, not merely repetition of inherited designs.

Mapuche silverwork includes the linked breast ornament trapelakucha, earrings called chaway and fastening pins such as tüpu. Specialists Antonio Chihuaicura and Marco Pailamilla examined such pieces with the museum, bringing makers’ knowledge to the interpretation of their construction and use.

Following nineteenth-century dispossession, families sometimes exchanged silver objects for food. The museum links these losses to the formation of public and private collections. An ornament’s museum history can therefore record hardship as well as artistic skill.

The same account describes craft knowledge surviving within families and being renewed through workshops, new pieces and replicas. Studying an old silver ornament and making a new one can both contribute to this continuing practice.

Potter Celinda Huaiquil explains links between water, women’s knowledge and ceramic vessels. Duck-shaped ketru metawe can pour liquids, including muday in ceremonies. Her interpretation joins close observation of living creatures with the practical work of shaping clay.

José Cayuqueo makes ritual drums using laurel wood and goatskin. He and Hernán Marinao also describe wooden pifüllka instruments accompanying the drum and supporting a machi’s ceremony. These are named makers’ accounts of living musical practice.

Manuel Manquilef’s writing and Pascual Coña’s orally narrated life preserve Mapuche perspectives on historical change. Coña’s account was recorded by a missionary, so the circumstances of recording matter alongside the narrator’s knowledge.

ending.text: Chilean and Argentine expansion dispossessed communities and restricted land and movement. Later migration brought many Mapuche people to cities. These transformations did not end Mapuche life: makers, teachers, families and organisations continue to sustain and reshape their cultures.

sources.note: Presentation: local autonomy, frontier exchange, dispossession and narrated history. Inconsistent dates in the older chronology are excluded.

sources.note: Presentation: lof, limited local authority and field allocation. This historical model is not universal for all communities and periods.
